title: The Early Elders
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: They are mentioned in Shabbat 64b: “The early elders said that she should not paint her eyes,” etc.; in Nazir 53a: “some of them used to say”; in Tosefta Ohalot 4:6 and 4:13; and in Tosefta Yadayim, chapter 2: “Rabbi Yose ben Durmaskit said: I was with the early elders when they came from Yavneh to Lod.”

In the Sifra, Vayikra, on “Or a soul”: “The early elders used to say: I might think even if he touched,” etc. In the Mekhilta, Beshalach, Massekhta deAmalek, beginning of chapter 2, they said: “So this measure goes through all the generations.”

Likewise “elders” without further designation are mentioned in the Mishnah and Gemara, as in Eruvin 8:7, Yoma 1:5, Zevachim 1:3, Yadayim 3:5 and 4:3, Tosefta Ohalot, chapter 18, and the Mekhilta, Beshalach, Massekhta deVayassa; and the elders of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, as in Eruvin 13b and Beitzah 4a.
Likewise Hillel and Shammai were called “elders.”

So too Rabban Gamliel the Elder (to distinguish him from Rabban Gamliel his grandson). Likewise they called Rabbi Yose HaGelili, Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehoshua “elders,” as explained in their entries.

Hyman notes that Rabbi always said of Rabbi Yose, “An elder has already ruled.” Hyman suggests that it is always a title for the greatest sage of the generation. The title “elder” is greater than “sage,” in Hyman’s reading of Taanit 16a, although the Gemara answers differently.

notes.text: The Yose ben Durmaskit expansion is distinct from Yehoshua in the named-elders list. Hyman’s always assertion and elder-versus-sage hierarchy remain his interpretation, including his explicit acknowledgment that the Gemara answers otherwise. Collective elders are not merged as a single person.

Shabbat 64b directly preserves the early elders’ prohibition and Akiva’s response. The collective elders are not merged as one individual. Hyman’s always assertion and elder-versus-sage hierarchy remain his interpretation, including his acknowledgment that the Gemara answers differently.
